content: When sarecycline is co-administered with P-glycoprotein (P-gp) inhibitors, close monitoring is required. Sarecycline can increase the levels or effects of drugs such as tolvaptan, topotecan, trabectedin, velpatasvir, vemurafenib, venetoclax, verapamil, vinblastine, vincristine, vincristine liposomal, and voxilaprevir by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. This may lead to toxicities associated with these P-gp substrates, potentially necessitating dosage adjustments. Caution and close monitoring are advised in these cases. The concurrent use of tretinoin with sarecycline is not recommended due to an increased risk of toxicity through an unknown mechanism. Additionally, combining oral retinoids with tetracyclines may elevate the risk of pseudotumor cerebri or intracranial hypertension. Alternative therapies should be considered, and close monitoring is essential if these drugs are used together. Trimagnesium citrate anhydrous and tripotassium dicitrato bismuthate can decrease the absorption and efficacy of sarecycline by impairing gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of these agents. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended, and dosing of tetracyclines should be separated from multivalent cation-containing products to avoid reduced efficacy. Zinc can also reduce the absorption and effectiveness of sarecycline by binding to it in the gastrointestinal tract. To mitigate this interaction, oral tetracycline derivatives and oral zinc salts should be administered at least two hours apart. Sarecycline may enhance the effects of vecuronium through pharmacodynamic synergism, increasing the risk of respiratory depression. Alternative drugs should be used, and close monitoring is advised if co-administration is unavoidable. Sarecycline use has been associated with several adverse effects and precautions. Vulvovaginal mycotic infections, vulvovaginal candidiasis, and hypersensitivity reactions to tetracyclines have been reported. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) is a potential complication of nearly all antibacterial agents, ranging from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Central nervous system side effects, such as light-headedness, dizziness, or vertigo, have been reported with tetracycline use. Patients experiencing these symptoms should be cautioned against driving or operating hazardous machinery. These symptoms may resolve during therapy or upon discontinuation of the drug. Photosensitivity reactions, such as exaggerated sunburn, have been observed with tetracyclines. Bacterial resistance to tetracyclines may develop, so these drugs should only be used as indicated. Overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, including fungi, may occur with antibiotic use. If superinfection develops, therapy should be discontinued, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Tetracyclines, including sarecycline, may cause discoloration of deciduous teeth and reversible inhibition of bone growth when administered during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. Pregnant women should discontinue sarecycline as soon as pregnancy is recognized. Tetracyclines are excreted in human milk, and due to the potential for serious adverse effects on bone and tooth development in nursing infants, sarecycline is not recommended for breastfeeding women. Sarecycline should be taken with or without food and swallowed with adequate fluid to reduce the risk of esophageal irritation or ulceration. It should be stored at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with excursions permitted to 15–30°C (59–86°F). The medication should be protected from moisture and excessive heat.
